lead: A curved beam is a member whose axis is already curved before it is loaded: a crane hook, the frame of a C-clamp or punch press, a chain link, a ring. When the depth of the section is not small compared with its radius of curvature, the straight-beam formula My/I is no longer right. The inner fibres are shorter than the outer ones, so the same rotation of the section strains them more: the stress varies hyperbolically, the neutral axis moves toward the centre of curvature, and the inner fibre carries the highest stress. This chapter gives the formulas and applies them to the crane hook and the C-frame.
prereq: You need bending stress and eccentric loading from combined loading.

blocks.text: In a straight beam all fibres between two sections have the same length, so the change in length, the strain and the stress all grow linearly with the distance from the neutral axis. In a curved beam a fibre at radius r between two sections at angle dφ has length r·dφ. When the sections rotate relative to each other, every fibre changes length by an amount proportional to its distance from the neutral axis, but the inner fibres started shorter. Dividing by the original length gives a strain, and so a stress, that is largest at the inner fibre and falls off as 1/r: a hyperbola.

With no net axial force from bending, the tension and compression must balance, which pulls the neutral axis toward the centre of curvature. It lies at radius R<sub>n</sub>, a distance e inside the centroidal radius R.
Rn = A/∫(dA/r); rectangle: Rn = h/ln(Ro/Ri); e = R − Rn

R<sub>i</sub> and R<sub>o</sub> are the inner and outer radii (mm); h = R<sub>o</sub> − R<sub>i</sub> is the depth and b the width of the rectangle (mm); A = bh is the area (mm²); R = R<sub>i</sub> + h/2 is the radius of the centroidal axis (mm). For a solid circle of diameter d, R<sub>n</sub> = (√R<sub>o</sub> + √R<sub>i</sub>)²/4. For a trapezium with width b<sub>i</sub> at the inner face and b<sub>o</sub> at the outer, R<sub>n</sub> = ½(b<sub>i</sub> + b<sub>o</sub>)h / {[(b<sub>i</sub>R<sub>o</sub> − b<sub>o</sub>R<sub>i</sub>)/h] ln(R<sub>o</sub>/R<sub>i</sub>) − (b<sub>i</sub> − b<sub>o</sub>)}; its centroid lies h(b<sub>i</sub> + 2b<sub>o</sub>)/[3(b<sub>i</sub> + b<sub>o</sub>)] from the inner face.

σ<sub>b</sub> is the bending stress (MPa) at a fibre of radius r (mm); M is the bending moment about the centroidal axis (N·mm), taken positive when it tends to straighten (open) the beam, as a load does on a hook. Positive σ<sub>b</sub> is tension.

At the inner fibre r = R<sub>i</sub>: σ<sub>bi</sub> = M(R<sub>n</sub> − R<sub>i</sub>)/(A·e·R<sub>i</sub>), tension. At the outer fibre r = R<sub>o</sub>: σ<sub>bo</sub> = −M(R<sub>o</sub> − R<sub>n</sub>)/(A·e·R<sub>o</sub>), compression. The small R<sub>i</sub> in the denominator is what raises the inner stress. A hook or frame section also carries the load as a direct pull, so the resultant stress is σ = P/A + σ<sub>b</sub> at each fibre. Some textbooks call this the Winkler–Bach theory. When h is small compared with R (h/R below about 0.2), e becomes tiny and the result approaches My/I.

In a crane hook the critical section is the horizontal section through the centre of curvature, the deepest part of the bend. The load line passes through the centre of curvature, so the moment about the centroid of that section is M = P·R. Hook sections are made trapezoidal, wide on the inside and narrow on the outside, to put more material where the tensile stress is high; a rectangular section is used here because its formula is short.

In a C-frame (a press, a riveter, a G-clamp) the load acts in the jaw at a distance a from the centre of curvature of the curved back, so M = P(a + R) about the centroidal axis of the curved section. The load tends to open the C, so the inner fibre at the throat is in tension, as in the hook. Figure 1.9.1 plots the stress across the hook section of the first example; the curved-beam curve is 36 % higher than the straight-beam line at the inner fibre.

items: Find R<sub>o</sub> = R<sub>i</sub> + h, A and R.
Find R<sub>n</sub> from the section formula and e = R − R<sub>n</sub>.
Find M about the centroidal axis: PR for a hook, P(a + R) for a C-frame.
Find σ<sub>bi</sub> and σ<sub>bo</sub>, add P/A to both, and check the larger against the allowable stress.

examples.question: A crane hook carries 20 kN. Its critical section is rectangular, 30 mm wide and 60 mm deep, with an inner radius of 40 mm, and the load line passes through the centre of curvature. Find the resultant stresses at the inner and outer fibres, and compare with the straight-beam formula.
steps: Outer fibre: σ<sub>bo</sub> = −1.40 × 10⁶ × (100 − 65.48)/(1800 × 4.52 × 100) = −59.4 MPa; resultant 11.11 − 59.4 = −48.3 MPa (compression).
Straight beam: Z = 30 × 60²/6 = 18,000 mm³, M/Z = 77.8 MPa, resultant 88.9 MPa at both faces. It under-estimates the inner stress by 120.8/88.9 = 1.36 times.
examples.answer: Inner fibre 120.8 MPa tension, outer fibre 48.3 MPa compression. The straight-beam formula would give 88.9 MPa, 26 % too low at the critical fibre.

examples.question: The curved back of a C-frame has a rectangular section 40 mm wide and 100 mm deep with an inner radius of 100 mm. A 20 kN load acts in the jaws along a line 150 mm from the centre of curvature. Find the resultant stresses at the inner and outer fibres.
steps: Inner fibre: σ<sub>bi</sub> = 6.0 × 10⁶ × 44.27/(4000 × 5.73 × 100) = 115.9 MPa; resultant 120.9 MPa tension.
Outer fibre: σ<sub>bo</sub> = −6.0 × 10⁶ × 55.73/(4000 × 5.73 × 200) = −72.9 MPa; resultant −67.9 MPa.
Straight beam for comparison: Z = 40 × 100²/6 = 66,667 mm³, M/Z = 90.0 MPa.
examples.answer: Inner fibre 120.9 MPa tension, outer fibre 67.9 MPa compression; the inner bending peak of 115.9 MPa is 29 % above the straight-beam value of 90.0 MPa.

traps: Using My/I for a deeply curved member: it under-estimates the inner-fibre stress.
Putting R instead of R<sub>n</sub> in the stress formula, or forgetting e = R − R<sub>n</sub>; e is small, so round it to at least two decimals.
Forgetting the direct stress P/A, or taking M = Pa instead of P(a + R) for a C-frame.
Taking the inner fibre of a hook as compressed. The load opens the hook, so the inner fibre is in tension.
Using diameters instead of radii, or mixing N·mm with m.

quiz.q: Write R<sub>n</sub> for a rectangular curved beam.
quiz.a: R<sub>n</sub> = h/ln(R<sub>o</sub>/R<sub>i</sub>), where h is the depth and R<sub>i</sub>, R<sub>o</sub> the inner and outer radii.

quiz.q: Give three machine parts analysed as curved beams.
quiz.a: Crane hooks, C-frames of presses and clamps, chain links (also rings and offset links).

quiz.q: Why is the bending stress highest at the inner fibre of a curved beam?
quiz.a: Inner fibres are shorter, so the same change in length gives a larger strain; the stress varies as (R<sub>n</sub> − r)/r and the neutral axis shifts inward, so the inner fibre has the largest stress.
The inner fibre carries the high tensile stress, so a wider inner face puts more material there, bringing the inner and outer stresses closer and saving mass.

quiz.q: A rectangular curved beam has b = 20 mm, h = 40 mm and R<sub>i</sub> = 20 mm. Find R<sub>n</sub> and e.
quiz.a: R<sub>o</sub> = 60 mm; R<sub>n</sub> = 40/ln 3 = 36.41 mm; R = 40 mm; e = 3.59 mm.

quiz.q: A curved beam has R<sub>n</sub> = 50 mm, e = 2 mm, A = 300 mm² and M = 60,000 N·mm. Find the bending stress at r = 40 mm.
A hook has h/R = 0.86 and passes a straight-beam check with a small margin. Is it safe?
quiz.a: Not necessarily. At this curvature the curved-beam inner stress is about a third higher than My/I (36 % in the worked example), so a small margin may vanish; it must be rechecked with the curved-beam formula.

beyond: Hooks are bought to standard shapes, proof-load tested and inspected for opening of the throat in service, which shows overload. Frames of presses are now checked by finite element analysis, which also captures the stress concentration at the throat and the stiffness of the C. Search next for crane hook standards, Winkler–Bach curved beam theory and C-frame press design.

figure.caption: Resultant stress across the crane-hook section of the first worked example (direct stress included). The curved-beam stress (solid) is a hyperbola that peaks at 120.8 MPa on the inner fibre; the straight-beam line (dashed) gives only 88.9 MPa there. The neutral axis of bending, at 65.48 mm, sits 4.52 mm inside the centroid.

spec.aria: Plot of stress against radius from 40 to 100 mm. Curved-beam curve from 120.8 MPa at the inner fibre down to minus 48.3 at the outer; straight-beam dashed line from 88.9 to minus 66.7. Vertical marks at the neutral-axis radius 65.48 and the centroid 70.
